extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent agents, and litigators (United Kingdom patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and practical criteria for assessing whether an invention is novel (i.e., not anticipated) under UK practice: prior uses, publications, disclosures (including prior patents/specifications), experimental use, secret use, and related doctrines that destroy or preserve novelty. Includes case examples and statutory note (Patents Act 1883).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use / anticipation by public user
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention or process has been publicly used in trade before the date of the patent, that public use is an anticipation and will invalidate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: five manufacturers openly practised a process (though not generally known) and the Court held there had been a public use so the patent was invalid. Public use includes commercial, non-experimental practice. The question at trial is whether the prior practice amounted to a public use (fact-specific). See Heath v. Smith and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior secret user (third party) — uncertain effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Secret user by a third party (use kept entirely secret but from which profit is derived) may deprive a subsequent patent of validity, but English courts have not conclusively adjudicated the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes that secret use 'from which the inventor derives a profit, and being not merely a user by way of experiment, will certainly deprive his after-acquired patent of its validity.' But the specific question whether prior secret user by someone other than the patentee suffices to vitiate a patent 'has never been judicially decided in an English court.' (Dictum of Mr Justice Erie in Heath v. Smith). Treat as a risky ground; case law uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior experimental use (experimental user exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Previous experiments, even if approaching the patented invention, do not necessarily invalidate a patent if they did not result in the utilization of the discovery and amounted only to experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish mere experiments (which leave the invention effectively unworked) from public use. A 'mere experiment' that does not complete or make the invention practically available will not prevent a later inventor from patenting a perfected result. But the boundary is delicate: slight differences in evidence may lead to opposite conclusions. Examples: Cornish v. Keene; Croll/Hills (gas purification) where jury found prior use experimental and not fatal. Jervis held warehousing for sale may be public not experimental—fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior imperfect machines / failed prior machines
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of an earlier machine that was imperfect or turned out a failure will not necessarily invalidate a later successful machine achieving the same object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior device was so imperfect as to be incapable of accomplishing the promised work, it will not deprive the later invention of novelty. Cases: Murray v. Clayton; Barlow v. Baylis. Courts look to whether the earlier device was 'incapable' or only imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earlier inventions with similar object but substantially different means
rubrics_metrics.description: A later patentee is not necessarily barred if an earlier inventor obtained a patent for a similar object, provided the earlier patentee had not secured the underlying principle and the means of accomplishing the object are substantially different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will compare principles and modes of operation: if modes are 'sufficiently distinct' the later invention can be valid. Examples: Kneller (evaporation apparatus) — same principle (forcing air through liquid) but different modes of effecting it led to no invalidity; Minter v. Brown (chairs) — different encumbering machinery may leave the later simplified principle patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication in printed books (prior printed disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior publication in a printed book that has been circulated in Great Britain and that discloses the invention will destroy novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prior printed description need not have been the source of the patentee's knowledge — public circulation suffices. Foreign books circulated or even a few copies can be sufficient if exposed for sale in England (cases cited where four copies sent to a bookseller sufficed). However, a single obscure copy in a depository or a book simply placed in a non-public inner library may not be sufficient publication (Plimpton; Ottó v. St.-L). The key is whether the description has become part of the 'public stock' of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication in prior patent specification (prior specification as anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior specification of another patent (whether expired or worthless) that describes the substance of the invention will deprive a later patent of novelty in the same way as a printed book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even an expired or worthless patent specification may sufficiently disclose an invention. If a prior specification enables the invention 'substantially' it anticipates. Example: M'Arthy pavement specification cut into parts anticipating later block patent; Lord Halsbury's remark in Kaye v. Chubb. Note: International priority rules (Art.4 and s.103 Patents Act 1883) limit application in some foreign-priority circumstances (footnote in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure requirement for prior publication to anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: For a prior publication (book or specification) to anticipate, it must provide such information that a person of ordinary skill would 'at once perceive, understand, and be able practically to apply the discovery' without needing further experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require prior disclosure to be 'equal' in practical utility to the later patent: specific necessary details for practical working must be substantially present in the prior disclosure. Apparent generality or theoretical statements that omit critical practical detail will not anticipate (see the long quotation from Wit»etbury and Brett LJ). Cases: Betts v. Menzies (general description insufficient), Otto v. Linford, Haslam v. Hall. Where a published drawing is itself sufficient for a mechanist to build the machine, that will invalidate the later patent (Lord Esher).

rubrics_metrics.name: General description vs practical invention (practical detail matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior general statement or speculative theory does not anticipate a later patent that supplies the practical and useful information necessary to carry the invention into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dobbs's early general patent for combining lead and tin lacked precision (thickness ratios, pressure), whereas Betts provided minute practical detail and the House of Lords upheld Betts's patent. If the antecedent publication does not contain the same amount of practical and useful information, it will not destroy novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of language and terms of art — meaning matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Even identical or verbatim language in two specifications does not automatically mean they describe the same external object; the terms of art used must have the same signification at both dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Westbury in Betts v. Menzies: must ascertain that the technical terms used in both documents denote the same external objects. Courts therefore construe specifications in light of contemporary technical meaning; verbatim text alone is not conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal continuity and abandonment of prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior public user relied on as invalidating need not have continued up to the date of the patent; even discontinued prior use can invalidate. But where prior use ceased long before and was completely lost sight of, courts have left open whether that would vitiate a later patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: House of Lords held discontinued prior user may invalidate (e.g., The Househill Co. v. Neilson), but also left open the special case where the thing had been long forgotten and 'completely lost sight of' until rediscovered. Evidence must clearly establish anticipation (Von Heyden v. Neustadt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical scope of prior user (colonial use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior user of an invention in a colony does not necessarily affect the validity of a patent subsequently obtained in the United Kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: decision cited (e.g., John v. H.) that prior user in a colony did not impair a UK patent. Geographic scope of prior use matters; publication or use must have made the invention part of UK's public stock to anticipate a British patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale or placing of articles in UK (imported articles) can anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale in England of articles made abroad may anticipate and thereby invalidate a subsequently patented invention in England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Jensen v. Smith. Placing articles in a warehouse for sale (even if no sale proved) has been held in at least one case to destroy novelty (penholders in warehouse — Jervis). Whether such conduct constitutes public disclosure/use is fact-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior publication by the inventor (self-disclosure) — waiving rights
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor who publishes or deals with the invention publicly before applying for a patent may disentitle himself to the patent: you cannot first publish your discovery and then obtain protection against the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law warns inventors to be cautious before applying. However, keeping the invention to oneself does not destroy the right provided there is no profitable user (Bentley v. Fleming). Depositing a machine in a room open to the public for a reasonable time for testing may be safe (Bentley v. Fleming). Bramall v. Hardcastle and other cases show limited internal manufacture prior to filing is not necessarily fatal. Advice: avoid public disclosures before filing unless provisional/priority protections apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional protection and fraud exception (Patents Act 1883 s.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 35 of the Patents Act 1883 provides that a patent granted to the true and first inventor shall not be invalidated by an application in fraud of him, or by provisional protection obtained thereon, or by any use or publication of the invention subsequent to that fraudulent application during the provisional period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory safeguard: fraudulent applications by others and certain provisional protections do not necessarily defeat a true inventor's later patent; consult the statute and subsequent amendments (note also international priority rules referred to elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior specification that omits practical details may not anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a prior provisional or earlier specification contained an incomplete description insufficient to enable a workman to make the object, it will not be treated as a prior publication invalidating a later complete specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a provisional specification omitted a piece of mechanism later included in the complete specification; courts held the earlier passage not sufficient to vitiate the later patent because it did not enable a workman to make the invention. This is an application of the enabling-disclosure test (see also Mulliner v. Hurt etc.).
